flawed_step: Any step that builds a Hamiltonian cycle of G from those of the vertex-deleted graphs G - v. The hypothesis does not support this, and hypohamiltonian graphs (such as the Petersen graph) show it cannot be done.
counterexample: Petersen graph on vertices 0..9: outer cycle 0-1-2-3-4-0, spokes i-(i+5), inner edges 5+i ~ 5+(i±2 mod 5) (inner cycle 5-7-9-6-8-5). G-0 has the Hamiltonian cycle 1-2-3-4-9-7-5-8-6-1. G-5 has 0-1-2-7-9-6-8-3-4-0. The rotation i->i+1, 5+i->5+i+1 (mod 5) is an automorphism, so every G-v is Hamiltonian. G is not: the spokes form an edge cut, so a Hamiltonian cycle uses 2 or 4 of them. With 2, the outer Hamiltonian path has ends i, i+1, and the inner path would need ends 5+i, 5+i+1, which are not adjacent on the inner cycle. With 4 (spoke j unused), the outer part is the paths (j-1,j,j+1) and (j+2,j+3), and the inner part is (5+j+3,5+j,5+j+2) and (5+j+1,5+j+4). Following the cycle closes the 5-cycle j+1 -> 5+j+1 -> 5+j+4 -> j-1 -> j -> j+1 before visiting all 10 vertices. Contradiction.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. The Petersen graph is hypohamiltonian: it is connected with 10 vertices, every vertex-deleted subgraph has a Hamiltonian cycle (explicit cycles for G-0 and G-5, extended to all vertices by the rotation automorphism), and G has no Hamiltonian cycle (shown by counting how many spokes a Hamiltonian cycle could use).
